items.name: World Wide Web
clues: It lets you jump from one document to another, anywhere in the world, with a single click.
A physics laboratory on the border between France and Switzerland, near Geneva.
A British computer scientist wrote a proposal for it in March 1989. His boss scribbled on it: “Vague but exciting”.
Its pages are written in HTML, sent with HTTP and found with a URL.
The very first server had a sticker on it: “This machine is a server. DO NOT POWER IT DOWN!!”
Three words that all start with W. People often confuse it with the internet itself.

items.name: Emoji
clues: It lets you show how you feel in a message without writing a single word.
A mobile phone company in Japan.
In 1999 a young designer drew a famous early set of 176 of them, each only 12 by 12 pixels.
Faces, hearts, food, weather, animals, an aubergine. Since 2010 they have been part of the same standard that computers use for letters.
That 1999 set is now in the Museum of Modern Art in New York. In 2015 Oxford Dictionaries named a later one, a face crying with laughter, its Word of the Year.
Japanese for “picture” plus “character”. Despite the sound, it has nothing to do with the English word “emotion”.

items.name: Hashtag
clues: It groups messages about the same topic, so that you can find them all at once.
A social network where every post was once limited to 140 characters.
A user suggested it in a short post in August 2007. The company reportedly told him that things like that were for nerds.
Activists, brands and TV shows all use it to start a campaign or a trend.
Americans call its symbol the pound sign. Its technical name is the octothorpe.
The symbol on your phone’s keypad, plus a word for a label: #likethis.

items.name: QR code
clues: It stores information that a machine can read in a fraction of a second.
A Japanese company that makes car parts, part of the Toyota group.
An engineer designed it in 1994 to keep track of parts on the production line.
During the pandemic it appeared on every restaurant table, instead of a menu.
Its inventor got the idea while playing Go, the board game with black and white stones.
A square of black and white dots with three bigger squares in the corners. Two letters: Q and R.

items.name: CAPTCHA
clues: It decides whether you may go any further, millions of times a day, and most people find it mildly annoying.
A university in Pittsburgh, in the United States.
Four computer scientists gave it its name in 2003. One of them later founded Duolingo.
You copy some wobbly letters, or click every square with a traffic light or a bus in it.
One version made people read words from old scanned books and newspapers, so millions of users helped to digitise them without knowing.
An acronym that ends “…to tell Computers and Humans Apart”. It asks: are you a robot?

items.name: Bluetooth
clues: It lets two devices talk to each other over a short distance without a cable.
Engineers at Ericsson, the Swedish telecoms company, in the 1990s.
In 1997 an engineer at Intel suggested a temporary code name for it after reading a novel about Vikings. The name stuck.
Wireless headphones, speakers, smartwatches and the car radio all use it.
Its logo combines two runes: the initials of a tenth-century king of Denmark and Norway.
It is named after that king’s nickname, which describes the colour of one of his teeth.
